turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a good market offer, but not yet a compelling “leave a job I like” offer. I would negotiate—not accept immediately and not walk away yet.**

On a simple four-year average:

| | Meta | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $235K |
| Target/typical bonus | $36K | $47K |
| Annualized equity | $250K | $270K |
| **Annualized TC** | **$526K** | **$552K** |

Google is offering only **$26K more per year, or about 5%**, on a normalized basis. Over four years, assuming flat stock prices, target bonuses, and no refreshes at either company, that is approximately **$2.208M at Google versus $2.104M at Meta**.

A 5% premium is thin compensation for:

- Leaving a company and role you like
- Taking execution, manager, team, and performance-rating risk
- Resetting your internal reputation and promotion trajectory
- Depending on uncertain refresh grants
- Potentially experiencing an equity cliff later

Your next 12 months at Meta are lower—about **$476K** because only $200K is scheduled to vest—so Google may look better in year one. But you should not let one temporarily lighter vesting year obscure the four-year economics.

For context, recent self-reported market data puts median Google L6 PM compensation around $514K, with a very wide range and a 90th percentile around $671K. Thus, $552K is respectable but not exceptional for an experienced Bay Area L6 PM. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

## The critical missing detail: vesting schedule

Before evaluating or countering, get the **exact new-hire vesting schedule and first vest date in writing**.

If it is 25% each year, your equity is $270K annually.

If it is front-loaded—for example, 38%/32%/20%/10%—the offer would look approximately like this before refreshes and stock-price changes:

| Year | Base + target bonus + initial RSUs |
|---|---:|
| Year 1 | $692K |
| Year 2 | $628K |
| Year 3 | $498K |
| Year 4 | $390K |

That would make years one and two attractive but create a serious cliff. Refreshes might soften it, but **you should assign no guaranteed value to refreshes**. Google’s own compensation-process description says equity refresh decisions depend on modeled recommendations, performance-related inputs, location, role, manager discretion, and higher-level review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Also confirm:

- Whether the bonus is prorated in your first year
- Whether you will be eligible for the next compensation/refresh cycle
- When the first RSUs vest
- Whether vesting is monthly or quarterly
- How the grant’s share count is determined
- Whether your anticipated start date affects refresh eligibility

## What I would ask for

### Opening counter

Ask for:

- **Base: $260K**
- **New-hire RSUs: $1.4M**
- **Sign-on bonus: $150K**

That produces approximately **$662K annualized before the sign-on**, versus $552K now. This is an opening anchor, not necessarily the expected landing point.

The base request is defensible: $235K is only about 59% of the way through the posted $183K–$271K range. You are already making $240K, you were not searching, and you are a directly comparable Meta IC6 PM. Other current Google Senior PM postings show similarly broad Bay Area base ranges plus 20% bonus and equity, so there is meaningful differentiation within the band. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS&utm_source=openai))

### Reasonable landing zone

I would target a final package around:

- **Base: $250K–$255K**
- **RSUs: $1.25M–$1.35M**
- **Sign-on: $100K–$150K**

At $255K base and $1.3M equity:

- Base: $255K
- Bonus: $51K
- Annualized initial equity: $325K
- **Annualized TC: approximately $631K**
- Plus sign-on

That is approximately a **20% premium over your normalized Meta compensation**, which is much more appropriate for a voluntary move from a situation you already like.

### Prioritize the components this way

1. **Equity**
2. **Sign-on**
3. **Base**

Equity has the largest effect on total compensation. Sign-on gives you guaranteed value and bridges forfeited Meta equity, bonus timing, or delayed vesting. Base is recurring and matters, but moving base from $235K to $255K only adds $24K annually including the corresponding 20% bonus increase.

If Google says it can move only one component, prioritize RSUs unless you strongly prefer guaranteed cash.

## Suggested script

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and role. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking, I’m happy at Meta, and this would need to represent a meaningful financial step forward for me to make the move.
>
> On a four-year annualized basis, the current offer is about $552K, compared with roughly $526K in my current role. That’s a relatively small premium given the transition risk and the fact that future equity refreshes aren’t guaranteed.
>
> I’d be ready to move forward if we could get the package closer to $260K base, $1.4M in new-hire equity, and a $150K sign-on bonus. I recognize there may be constraints across individual components, so I’m open to how the package is structured, but I would need the overall guaranteed value to move meaningfully.
>
> Could you take that back to the compensation team?

If they ask what you are forfeiting:

> I have approximately $200K of Meta equity scheduled to vest over the next 12 months, along with my existing bonus and future compensation trajectory. More broadly, because I’m not looking to leave, I’m evaluating the package against both my current compensation and the risk of resetting at a new company.

Do **not** say, “I’ll accept if you give me X,” unless you truly will. Use “I’d be ready to move forward” or “that would get us much closer.”

## Also negotiate the start date

Look at your Meta vest dates. If a meaningful tranche vests soon, ask Google to let you start immediately after that vest.

For example, preserving a $50K Meta vest by delaying your start a few weeks is economically equivalent to securing another $50K sign-on, without requiring Google’s compensation team to approve more money.

Do not resign until:

- The revised offer is written
- The vesting schedule is confirmed
- The grant amount and sign-on are documented
- The start date protects any nearby Meta vest where possible

## My decision thresholds

### Accept

I would seriously consider accepting if Google reaches roughly:

- **$610K–$630K+ annualized guaranteed target compensation**, or
- A slightly lower recurring package combined with **$100K–$150K sign-on**, provided the role is at least as attractive as Meta

Example: $250K base, $50K bonus, $1.25M equity, and $100K sign-on equals $612.5K annualized before the sign-on.

### Consider, based on the job

If they reach approximately **$590K–$610K**, it becomes a balanced decision. Take it only if the manager, scope, product area, work-life balance, or long-term trajectory is clearly better.

### Stay at Meta

If Google makes little or no improvement and the role itself is not substantially better, **stay**. The current $552K package is competitive in the abstract, but it does not adequately compensate someone who:

- Already earns $526K
- Likes their current role
- Was not looking
- Has no urgent reason to leave

## Recommendation

**Counter at $260K base, $1.4M RSUs, and $150K sign-on. Aim to land around $250K–$255K base, $1.25M–$1.35M RSUs, and $100K–$150K sign-on.**

If Google remains at or close to the original offer, I would decline unless the role is materially better for nonfinancial reasons. The current offer is **good**, but for you specifically it is not yet **good enough to switch**.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs stay at $1,080,000, plus a $200,000 sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation

**Yes—I would take it, provided you’re genuinely comfortable with the manager, team, scope, and work-life expectations.**

Financially, the $200K sign-on moves this from a marginal offer to a solid switching package. If you strongly prefer your current Meta role, staying remains reasonable—but I would no longer reject Google because the compensation is inadequate.

## The economics

Assuming $1.08M vests evenly over four years:

|  | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Bonus | ~$36K | $48K target |
| Annualized initial equity | ~$250K | $270K |
| **Ongoing annualized TC** | **$526K** | **$558K** |
| Sign-on | — | **$200K** |

### Four-year view

- **Meta:** approximately $2.104M
- **Google:** approximately $2.432M
- **Google advantage:** approximately **$328K gross**
- **Four-year average at Google:** approximately **$608K/year**
- **Average premium over Meta:** approximately **15.6%**

That is now a reasonable premium for switching companies.

### First 12 months

Using your numbers:

- Stay at Meta: approximately **$476K**
- Google: potentially approximately **$758K**, assuming a full target bonus, $270K of vesting, and the full sign-on
- Potential difference: approximately **$282K**

The actual first-year figure may be lower if the bonus is prorated, the equity schedule is uneven, or the sign-on is paid in installments.

## The important nuance

The **ongoing** offer after the sign-on is only:

> $240K base + $48K target bonus + $270K annualized RSUs = **$558K**

That is only about **$32K, or 6%, above your current $526K**. Therefore:

- The **$200K sign-on is what makes the switch worthwhile**
- This is not a dramatic long-term recurring-pay increase
- You should not count future Google refreshes in your decision
- If Meta is likely to increase your equity or promote you soon, the long-term advantage could disappear
- Conversely, Google refreshes could improve the economics, but they should be treated as upside

Alphabet states that RSUs generally vest over four years and remain contingent on employment at each vesting date, reinforcing the need to understand the exact schedule. ([abc.xyz](https://abc.xyz/assets/99/21/46cafdba41089a12a2d86ea47d44/goog026-annualreport2024-web.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Before signing, confirm these items in writing

### 1. Sign-on payment and repayment terms

Specifically:

- When is the $200K paid?
- Is it all paid in the first paycheck, or split across multiple years?
- Is repayment required if you voluntarily leave?
- Is the clawback 12 months, 24 months, or longer?
- Is repayment prorated or all-or-nothing?
- Is repayment based on the **gross** $200K even though you receive a smaller net payment?

A two-year, non-prorated clawback would make the offer meaningfully less attractive because it effectively ties you to the role.

### 2. Exact RSU vesting schedule

Confirm:

- First vesting date
- Monthly versus quarterly vesting
- Whether the grant is even or front-loaded
- How the number of shares is calculated
- Whether there is any delay between starting and receiving the grant

Do not rely only on “$270K per year” arithmetic until you see the actual schedule.

### 3. First-year bonus eligibility

Confirm whether:

- The $48K target bonus is prorated
- You will be eligible for the next performance cycle
- Your start date affects bonus or refresh eligibility

### 4. Start date

If you have a meaningful Meta vest coming soon, try to start immediately after it. Even if compensation is closed, **start date may still be negotiable**.

### 5. Offer expiration and contingencies

Do not resign until:

- The written offer is final
- The sign-on is documented
- The vest schedule is documented
- Background checks and other contingencies are understood
- Your start date is agreed upon

## Don’t overreact to the sign-on’s withholding

The cash bonus may appear to be taxed heavily because supplemental-wage withholding can differ from ordinary paycheck withholding. But withholding is not necessarily your ultimate tax rate: bonuses are taxable compensation, and RSUs are generally treated as wages for federal withholding purposes as well. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p505?utm_source=openai))

In other words, don’t mentally value the $200K sign-on at zero because the net deposit is much smaller. Compare gross compensation to gross compensation, then plan separately for taxes.

## When I would decline despite the money

I would stay at Meta if any of these are true:

- You materially prefer your current manager or team
- The Google scope feels narrower or less promotable
- The team has concerning attrition or reorganization risk
- Work-life balance is likely to be considerably worse
- You are close to a credible promotion or major compensation reset at Meta
- You would be taking Google only for the sign-on and already expect to want to leave within a year
- The sign-on has a punitive two-year, non-prorated clawback

A one-time $200K payment is not enough to tolerate a substantially worse job.

## Final answer

**If the Google role is at least roughly as attractive as your Meta role, take it.** You negotiated successfully: the revised package is worth approximately $328K more over four years under reasonable static assumptions, and the $200K sign-on protects the economics of leaving your near-term Meta vesting behind.

**If you clearly prefer staying at Meta, don’t let the sign-on force the move.** The ongoing compensation premium is only about 6%, so this is financially compelling but not financially irresistible.

Since they have stated this is the final offer, I would **not issue another compensation counter**. I would limit any remaining requests to start date, sign-on repayment structure, and written clarification of vesting and bonus terms.
